title: Network attacks and defences
summary: How attackers abuse ARP, DHCP, VLANs, DNS, BGP and TCP, how floods and amplification work, and how switches, DNSSEC, RPKI, firewalls, segmentation and IDS stop or reveal them, with real cases.
outcomes: Explain what on-path, off-path and local-network attackers can do, and why switching alone does not stop sniffing
Explain how DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection and 802.1X stop ARP spoofing, rogue DHCP and unauthorised devices
Compute DNS cache poisoning odds, including the birthday effect, and explain how Kaminsky's 2008 attack and its fixes work
Classify BGP hijacks and route leaks and decide a route's RPKI validation state as Valid, Invalid or NotFound
Explain SYN floods, SYN cookies, blind RST injection and challenge ACKs, with the numbers behind each
Compute amplification factors and attacker bandwidth, and describe scrubbing, anycast and HTTP/2 Rapid Reset defences
Recognise scanning, floods, tunnelling and exfiltration in Zeek logs, flow records and Suricata alerts
Design firewall rules, segmentation and zero trust access that would have contained a breach like Target 2013

lessons.title: Where the attacker stands: on-path, off-path and on your LAN

blocks.md:
Every network attack starts with one question: **where is the attacker, relative to the packets?** Picture a café. Ana's laptop talks to a bank's server. The café's Wi-Fi router, the café's internet provider and every router after it all handle Ana's packets. A stranger at the next table handles none of them, but shares the same local network. Someone in another country handles none of them and shares nothing.

These three people can do very different things, and most defences only make sense once you know which one you are stopping.

RFC 3552, the IETF's guide to writing security sections for protocols (an RFC, Request for Comments, is a numbered internet standards document), gives the vocabulary used throughout this course:

- A **passive attack** only reads packets (for example sniffing, which means recording traffic that passes you). An **active attack** also writes: it sends, changes, drops or replays packets.
- An **on-path** attacker sits on the route the packets take, like a router, so it can "read, modify, or remove any datagram transmitted along that path". Older texts call this man-in-the-middle.
- An **off-path** attacker can send packets that "appear to come from any hosts" (spoofing) but cannot see replies. To read traffic it must first "subvert the topology" to get on-path.

blocks.title: Three attacker positions around one connection

scenes.caption: Ana's packets cross the café router, then the ISP's routers, then reach the bank. Each box on that line is on-path.
On-path: the ISP's routers handle every packet, so they can read, delay, drop or rewrite them. This is the strongest position.
Off-path: the remote attacker can send forged packets to the bank, but replies go to the real address. It must guess anything it cannot see, such as sequence numbers.
Local network: the stranger is not on the path yet, but can speak LAN protocols (ARP, DHCP) that were built to trust neighbours. Lessons 2 and 3 show how that turns into on-path.

blocks.md:
**Sniffing and switches.** On an old shared hub every frame reached every port. A **switch** (recalled from the prerequisite: it learns which MAC address lives on which port and forwards frames only there) seems to fix sniffing. It does not, for four reasons:

1. **Flooded and broadcast traffic** still reaches everyone: broadcasts, and frames to MAC addresses the switch has not learned yet.
2. **Table overflow.** The switch documentation of Juniper Networks, a maker of routers and switches, describes an attack where an intruder "sends so many requests from new MAC addresses that the table cannot learn all the addresses". The switch then floods frames to all ports, and "the attacker might also be able to sniff that broadcast traffic".
3. **ARP and DHCP tricks** (next two lessons) make victims send their frames to the attacker on purpose.
4. **Shared media** such as Wi-Fi put every nearby radio in range (the Wireless and mobile security course covers it).

blocks.title: A switch MAC table overflowing (toy table of 4 entries)

scenes.caption: Simplified: real tables hold thousands of entries. Two hosts are learned. A frame for B goes only to port 2, so a sniffer on port 3 sees nothing.
A device on port 3 sends frames from many invented source MACs. Each one is learned, filling the free slots.
Old entries age out and are replaced by more invented MACs. B's entry is gone.
A frame for B now has no table entry, so the switch floods it out of every port, including port 3. The switch has fallen back to behaving like a hub.

blocks.code:
# Toy model of a learning switch with a tiny MAC table, to see why overflow
# turns unicast into flooding. Not a real switch: real tables age entries out.
from collections import OrderedDict

class Switch:
    def __init__(self, size, ports):
        self.table, self.size, self.ports = OrderedDict(), size, ports

    def frame(self, src, dst, in_port):
        self.table.pop(src, None)
        if len(self.table) >= self.size:
            self.table.popitem(last=False)        # evict the oldest entry
        self.table[src] = in_port                 # learn where src lives
        if dst in self.table:
            return [self.table[dst]]              # known: one port only
        return [p for p in self.ports if p != in_port]   # unknown: flood

sw = Switch(size=4, ports=[1, 2, 3, 4])
sw.frame("A", "B", 1); sw.frame("B", "A", 2)
print(sw.frame("A", "B", 1))        # [2]: only B's port
for i in range(4):                   # port 3 sends from 4 invented MACs
    sw.frame(f"X{i}", "A", 3)
print(sw.frame("A", "B", 1))        # [2, 3, 4]: B forgotten, frame flooded
blocks.caption: Runs as is. The second print shows port 3 receiving B's traffic once the table is full of invented addresses. Simplified: this toy evicts the oldest entry to make room; a real full table stops learning, and B is lost when its entry ages out, as in the figure.

blocks.md:
**Defender's view.** Switches can cap how many MAC addresses one port may learn. Juniper calls this **MAC limiting** and recommends it together with a list of explicitly allowed MACs for critical devices, so their entries cannot be pushed out. The signals to watch: one access port suddenly announcing hundreds of new MAC addresses, and MAC-limit violation messages in the switch's system log.

The broader lesson: a switch is a performance device that happens to reduce exposure. Treat the local network as a place where an attacker can be, and protect the traffic itself with encryption.

Know the position before you pick the defence. Encryption (TLS) defeats on-path reading and rewriting of content. Unpredictable numbers (random ports, sequence numbers, IDs) defeat off-path guessing. Switch features such as MAC limiting, DHCP snooping and ARP inspection stop local attackers from becoming on-path.

blocks.question: A host 3,000 km away sends a packet with a forged source address to your server. Which statement is true?
options: It is on-path, because its packet reached your server
It will receive your server's reply, because the source address is in the packet
It cannot reach your server at all without being on the same LAN
It cannot see the reply, so any secret your server puts in the reply (such as a sequence number) must be guessed
blocks.explain: Replies go to the forged address, not to the sender. That is the defining limit of an off-path attacker, and why protocols put unguessable values (TCP sequence numbers, DNS transaction IDs) in places only the real peer can see.

blocks.question: Your office uses only switches, no hubs. A colleague says sniffing is therefore impossible on the office LAN. What is the best reply?
options: Wrong, because switches copy every frame to a monitoring port by default
Wrong: broadcasts and unknown destinations are flooded, table overflow can force flooding, and ARP or DHCP tricks can redirect frames to an attacker
Wrong, but only for Wi-Fi users
Correct: switches send each frame only to its destination port
blocks.explain: Switching reduces what a sniffer sees but does not stop a local attacker. Flooding, MAC table overflow and redirection attacks all deliver other people's frames to the attacker's port. Mirror ports exist but are configured by administrators, not on by default.

lessons.title: ARP spoofing up close, and how switches stop it

blocks.md:
Recall from the prerequisite: **ARP** (Address Resolution Protocol, RFC 826) turns an IP address into a MAC address on the local network, and a host overwrites its cache with whatever an ARP packet claims, even unasked. One forged reply redirects one direction of traffic. This lesson follows the full attack and then the switch features built to stop it.

Tiny example: Ana's laptop is `192.168.1.23`, the router is `192.168.1.1`, and Mallory (the conventional name for an active attacker) is `192.168.1.66` on the same switch.

**Getting fully in the middle.** Juniper's documentation describes ARP spoofing as "one way to initiate man-in-the-middle attacks": the attacker sends ARP packets that claim another device's IP address with the attacker's own MAC. To capture both directions the attacker poisons two caches:

- tell Ana that `192.168.1.1` is at Mallory's MAC, and
- tell the router that `192.168.1.23` is at Mallory's MAC.

If Mallory then passes each frame on to the real destination, both sides keep working and notice nothing. Mallory is now on-path for everything Ana sends off the LAN. A related form is the **gratuitous ARP**: an unrequested ARP announcement about an address, normally sent after a network card changes, which a poisoner can abuse the same way.

blocks.title: Two forged replies put Mallory between Ana and the router

scenes.caption: Normal state: Ana's cache maps .1 to the router's MAC, the router maps .23 to Ana's MAC. Frames go straight between them.
Mallory sends Ana an ARP reply: '.1 is at Mallory's MAC'. RFC 826 lets it overwrite the existing entry.
Mallory sends the router a matching lie about Ana. Both directions are now poisoned.
Ana's next frame for the internet goes to Mallory, who reads it and passes it on. The router's replies take the same detour back.
The attacker must keep re-sending the lies, because real ARP traffic would otherwise repair the caches. That steady repetition is one of the signals defenders see.

blocks.md: **What the attacker gets.** Anything unencrypted: old protocols that send passwords in clear text, plain HTTP pages and cookies, DNS questions and answers (which can also be altered, sending Ana to a fake site). Against well-configured HTTPS the attacker mostly sees metadata and ciphertext, as the prerequisite's TLS lesson explained. That is why ARP spoofing today is usually a first step: get on-path, then attack DNS, downgrade connections or harvest plaintext from internal systems.

**The switch defences.** Two features work together, described here from Juniper's documentation (other vendors have equivalents under the same names):

- **DHCP snooping** watches DHCP exchanges and builds a **binding table**: for each lease on an untrusted port it records the MAC address, IP address, lease time, VLAN and interface. Ports toward real DHCP servers are marked *trusted*; on Juniper switches access ports are untrusted and trunk ports (links to other switches) trusted by default.
- **Dynamic ARP inspection (DAI)** intercepts ARP packets arriving on untrusted ports and checks them against that table. "If no IP-MAC entry in the database corresponds to the information in the ARP packet, DAI drops the ARP packet", the cache is not updated, and a system log message is recorded. DAI is enabled per VLAN and is off by default.

A host with a static address has no DHCP binding, so it needs a static entry, or DAI will drop its legitimate ARP.

blocks.title: Dynamic ARP inspection, as a function
blocks.code:
bindings = {  # built by DHCP snooping: (ip, vlan) -> (mac, port)
    ("192.168.1.23", 10): ("00:00:5e:00:53:23", "ge-0/0/3"),
    ("192.168.1.66", 10): ("00:00:5e:00:53:66", "ge-0/0/7"),
}
TRUSTED = {"ge-0/0/47"}      # uplink toward the router and DHCP server

def inspect_arp(sender_ip, sender_mac, vlan, port):
    if port in TRUSTED:
        return "forward"
    entry = bindings.get((sender_ip, vlan))
    if entry == (sender_mac, port):
        return "forward"
    return "drop and log"

print(inspect_arp("192.168.1.23", "00:00:5e:00:53:23", 10, "ge-0/0/3"))
print(inspect_arp("192.168.1.1", "00:00:5e:00:53:66", 10, "ge-0/0/7"))

scenes.caption: The binding table comes from DHCP snooping: who leased which address, with which MAC, on which port.
Ana's own ARP announcement arrives on Ana's port. Not a trusted port, so it is checked.
The table entry matches both the MAC and the port, so the ARP packet is forwarded.
Mallory claims the router's address .1 from port ge-0/0/7. There is no lease for .1 on this port with this MAC.
No match, so the forged ARP is dropped and logged. Ana's cache is never touched.

blocks.code:
# Junos (ELS style) for a VLAN named staff: trust the uplink port,
# turn on DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection for the VLAN.
set vlans staff forwarding-options dhcp-security group uplink interface ge-0/0/47.0
set vlans staff forwarding-options dhcp-security group uplink overrides trusted
set vlans staff forwarding-options dhcp-security arp-inspection
blocks.caption: Configuration form taken from Juniper's DAI and trusted DHCP server documentation. Port names are examples. Configuring DHCP security on a VLAN enables DHCP snooping for it.

blocks.md: **Detection without DAI.** Where switches cannot inspect ARP, watch the traffic itself. Signals: one IP address claimed by two different MAC addresses in a short time (Wireshark flags this as `arp.duplicate-address-detected`); a host's gateway MAC changing; one MAC claiming many IP addresses; a steady stream of unsolicited ARP replies from one port. Response: find the port the attacker's MAC is learned on and shut it, then review what crossed the network unencrypted while it was poisoned.

Static ARP entries on every laptop are not a practical fix: they break when hardware changes and do not scale. Put the check in the switch (DHCP snooping plus DAI), where one configuration covers every port, and encrypt traffic so a successful poisoner learns little.

blocks.question: DAI is enabled on a VLAN, but a server with a manually configured (static) IP address suddenly cannot be reached. What is the most likely cause?
options: The server's MAC address is too long
DAI only works on trunk ports
DAI blocks all servers by design
The server's ARP packets are dropped because DHCP snooping never saw a lease for it, so it has no binding
blocks.explain: DAI validates ARP against the DHCP snooping table. A statically addressed host never leased its address, so its ARP fails the check. The fix is a static binding (or ARP access list) for that host, or a trusted port where appropriate.

blocks.question: Mallory poisons only Ana's cache (telling Ana that the router's IP is at Mallory's MAC) and relays frames. What does Mallory see?
options: Only broadcast frames
Both directions of Ana's internet traffic
Ana's outgoing frames to the internet, but not the replies, which the router sends straight to Ana
Nothing, because the router still knows Ana's real MAC
blocks.explain: ARP poisoning is per direction. Ana's cache now sends Ana's frames to Mallory, but the router's cache is untouched, so replies go directly to Ana. To sit fully in the middle an attacker must poison both caches, which is exactly what doubles the signal for defenders.

lessons.title: DHCP starvation and rogue DHCP servers

blocks.md:
**DHCP** (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) hands a joining device its IP address, its default gateway and its DNS server, as the prerequisite showed. Whoever answers DHCP therefore decides where the device sends all its traffic and all its name lookups. Two attacks follow from that, and Juniper's port security documentation describes both.

Tiny example: an office VLAN has a DHCP server with a pool of 8 addresses (real pools are larger; a /24 subnet has 254 usable host addresses).

**DHCP starvation.** "An attacker floods an Ethernet LAN with DHCP requests from spoofed (counterfeit) MAC addresses" until the server's address pool "is completely used up". New, legitimate clients then get no address, which is a denial of service.

**Rogue DHCP server.** An attacker runs their own DHCP server on the LAN. It "can start issuing leases to the network's DHCP clients", and the leases can name the attacker's machine as default gateway or DNS server, which makes the attacker on-path for every device that accepts them. Clients usually take the first offer that arrives, so the two attacks combine well: starve the real server, then be the only one answering.

blocks.title: A DHCP pool of 8 addresses being starved (toy pool)

scenes.caption: The pool starts with 8 free addresses. Each lease is tied to the MAC address in the client's request.
Two real employees join and get leases.
One port sends DHCP requests from six invented MAC addresses. The server cannot tell them from real clients and leases them all.
Chen arrives. The pool is exhausted, so Chen gets no address from the real server. A rogue server's offer is now the only one Chen will receive.

blocks.title: DHCP snooping drops the rogue offer

scenes.caption: The laptop broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER. The switch floods broadcasts, so both servers hear it.
Without snooping: the rogue answers first, offering itself as gateway and DNS. The laptop takes the first offer.
With DHCP snooping the rogue's port is untrusted. Server messages (OFFER, ACK) arriving there are dropped and logged.
The real server's offer arrives on the trusted uplink and is forwarded. The laptop completes the exchange and the switch records the binding.

blocks.md:
**Defences, mapped to each attack** (Juniper's recommendations):

- Against the rogue server: **DHCP snooping** with only the real server's port trusted. Juniper: "If the DHCPOFFER packet is from a trusted interface, the switch forwards the packet"; untrusted ports drop DHCP server traffic, and the switch logs server messages seen there.
- Against starvation: **MAC limiting**, a cap on how many MAC addresses one access port may learn, so one port cannot claim the whole pool.
- **DHCP option 82** (the Relay Agent Information option: the switch adds which port and switch a request came from) lets the server apply per-port policy and helps against address spoofing and starvation.
- **802.1X** (next lesson) stops unknown devices from getting a lease at all.

blocks.code:
5 untrusted DHCPOFFER received, interface ge-0/0/0.0[65], vlan v1[10] server ip/mac
12.12.12.1/00:00:00:00:01:12 offer ip/client mac 12.12.12.253/00:AA:BB:CC:DD:01
blocks.caption: A Juniper switch log message, quoted from its documentation: five DHCP offers arrived on an untrusted port. It names the port, VLAN, the rogue server's IP and MAC, and the client it tried to serve.

blocks.md: **Defender's view.** Reading that log line is incident response in miniature: the interface tells you which wall socket to visit, the server IP and MAC identify the device, and the client MAC tells you who may have accepted a bad lease. Other signals: DHCP pool utilisation jumping to 100 percent in minutes, hundreds of leases to MAC addresses never seen before, and clients reporting a gateway or DNS server that is not yours. Response: shut the port, release the rogue leases, and check affected clients' DNS and gateway settings.
Whoever answers DHCP chooses a device's gateway and DNS server, so a rogue DHCP server is an on-path attack on every device it reaches. Only trusted ports may send DHCP server messages.

blocks.question: A switch has DHCP snooping on, but the real DHCP server was plugged into an access port that nobody marked trusted. What happens?
options: The real server's offers are dropped like a rogue's, so clients get no addresses until the port is marked trusted
Nothing changes, snooping only logs
The switch automatically trusts the first server it hears
Clients get addresses faster
blocks.explain: Snooping drops server messages on untrusted ports, whoever sends them. Juniper's documentation says that a DHCP server attached to an access port must have that port configured as trusted.

lessons.title: VLANs, VLAN hopping and 802.1X port authentication

blocks.md:
A **VLAN** (virtual local area network) lets one physical switch act as several separate LANs. Each frame carries, or is assigned, a VLAN number, and the switch keeps VLANs apart: a host on VLAN 1 cannot reach a host on VLAN 2 except through a router or firewall, where rules can apply. Networks use VLANs to keep, say, guests, staff, printers and payment terminals apart. The IEEE standard for VLAN tagging is 802.1Q, so tagged frames are often called "dot1q" frames.

Two kinds of switch port matter:
- An **access port** connects one end device and belongs to one VLAN. The device sends ordinary untagged frames.
- A **trunk port** connects switches (or a switch and a router) and carries many VLANs, each frame tagged with its VLAN number. A trunk can also be set up with one **native VLAN** whose frames cross it untagged: an untagged frame arriving on the trunk is put into that VLAN ([Juniper's VLAN guide](https://www.juniper.net/documentation/us/en/software/junos/multicast-l2/topics/topic-map/bridging-and-vlans.html)).

**VLAN hopping** means sending traffic into a VLAN you are not on, skipping the router where the rules live. A LevelBlue (formerly AT&T Cybersecurity) explainer describes the two classic forms:

- **Switch spoofing.** DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol), a proprietary protocol of the network equipment maker Cisco, lets two switches agree automatically to form a trunk. If an access port is left in a negotiating mode ("dynamic desirable", "dynamic auto" or "trunk"), a host can pretend to be a switch, get a trunk, and then reach every VLAN on it.
- **Double tagging.** A frame carries two VLAN tags. The first switch removes only the outer tag (the native VLAN's) and forwards the frame over a trunk; the next switch reads the inner tag and delivers it into the victim VLAN. It only works if the sender is on the trunk's native VLAN, and it is one-way, since replies cannot come back the same route.

blocks.title: Double tagging: one tag is peeled off at each switch

scenes.caption: Simplified. The sender sits on VLAN 1, which is also the trunk's native VLAN, and builds a frame with two tags: outer 1, inner 20 (the payment VLAN).
Switch 1 accepts it on VLAN 1 and removes the outer tag. Native VLAN frames cross the trunk untagged, so it sends the rest as is.
Switch 2 receives a frame on the trunk that now carries tag 20 and delivers it into VLAN 20. The frame skipped the router and its rules. Replies cannot return this way.

blocks.md:
**Fixes** are configuration hygiene: set every port that faces end devices to fixed access mode with negotiation off; make the native VLAN of every trunk a VLAN that no user port belongs to; and do not put users on the default VLAN. Defenders can also audit configurations: any access port in a dynamic trunking mode is a finding.

Remember what a VLAN is for: it separates broadcast domains so that a router or firewall can enforce rules between them. The rules live in that firewall, not in the VLAN number (lesson 16 returns to this).

**802.1X: who may plug in at all.** Everything so far assumed the attacker can plug into a port and get an address. **IEEE 802.1X** (the IEEE's standard for *port-based network access control*) closes that door. In Juniper's description the switch is the **authenticator**: it blocks all traffic from the device (the **supplicant**) at the port "until the supplicant's credentials are presented and matched on the authentication server (a RADIUS server)". RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is the long-standing protocol switches and VPNs use to ask a central server "is this user allowed?".

The device and switch speak **EAP over LAN** (EAPoL; EAP is the Extensible Authentication Protocol, a framework that carries many login methods such as certificates). Authenticating "before they receive an IP address from a DHCP server prevents unauthorized supplicants from gaining access". The server can also place the device in a specific VLAN.

blocks.title: 802.1X: the port stays closed until RADIUS says yes

scenes.caption: The laptop plugs in. The port forwards nothing except authentication frames.
The switch asks who it is; the answer is relayed to the RADIUS server inside RADIUS messages.
The EAP method runs end to end between laptop and server, for example EAP-TLS with a device certificate.
The server accepts, optionally naming a VLAN. Only now does the switch open the port, and only now can the laptop send DHCP.

blocks.md: 802.1X checks a device when the port opens, not every frame. Juniper's single supplicant mode authenticates only the first device and then lets others behind it through, so prefer single-secure or multiple supplicant mode. Even those then admit frames by source MAC address, so a bridge slipped in behind a real device can ride its session. Where that matters, add MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE), which authenticates and encrypts every frame on the link, and keep DHCP snooping and ARP inspection on.

blocks.question: A trunk's native VLAN is 1 and the guest Wi-Fi bridge is also on VLAN 1. Which change best removes the double-tagging risk?
options: Add more VLANs
Turn on DHCP snooping
Give the trunk a native VLAN that no user or guest port uses
Move the payment terminals to VLAN 2
blocks.explain: Double tagging needs the sender to be on the trunk's native VLAN, because that is the tag the first switch strips. Making the native VLAN one with no user ports removes the precondition. The other options do not touch the tag handling.

blocks.question: Why does 802.1X authenticate a device before DHCP rather than after?
options: To make DHCP faster
So that an unauthorised device never gets an address, a gateway or any traffic onto the LAN, which also blocks it from DHCP and ARP attacks
DHCP cannot work on authenticated ports
Because RADIUS servers need the device's IP address
blocks.explain: With the port closed until authentication, an unknown device cannot even attempt DHCP starvation, rogue offers or ARP spoofing. Authentication first is what makes it an access-control boundary.

lessons.title: DNS cache poisoning: the race and the birthday maths

blocks.md:
A recursive resolver (recalled from the prerequisite: the server that looks names up on your behalf and caches the answers) sends a question over UDP and must decide which reply is genuine. Poison its cache once and every user of that resolver is sent to the attacker's address until the record expires. This lesson does the maths of how hard that is, using the model in RFC 5452 ("Measures for Making DNS More Resilient against Forged Answers", 2009).

Tiny example: the resolver asks the authoritative server for `www.bank.example`. An off-path attacker cannot see the question, so they send forged answers and hope one matches before the real one arrives.

**What a forged reply must match.** Steve Friedl, a software consultant, in his illustrated guide to the Kaminsky bug (Unixwiz.net Tech Tips, August 2008), lists a resolver's acceptance rules: the reply arrives on the UDP port the query was sent from; its question section matches the pending query; its 16-bit **query ID** (transaction ID) matches; and its extra records are in the same domain as the question, which is called **bailiwick checking** (a [bailiwick](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/bailiwick) is the district where a bailiff has jurisdiction, so: only data about your own domain is accepted). It must also come from the server's address, which spoofing provides, and arrive first: "the real answer that arrives later is dropped". The time between the question leaving and the real answer arriving is the **window of opportunity**.

blocks.tex: P_s = \frac{D \cdot F}{N \cdot P \cdot I} \qquad P_{cs} = 1 - (1 - P_s)^{T/\mathrm{TTL}}
blocks.caption: RFC 5452: F forged packets land in one window; I = 65,536 query IDs; P = source ports used; N = authoritative servers; D = identical queries outstanding. Over time T the attacker gets a fresh window each time the record's TTL expires.

blocks.md: Read the formula as "guesses landed divided by the size of the haystack". With a fixed source port ($P = 1$), the haystack is only $N \cdot 65{,}536$. RFC 5452's worked example: an attacker sending 7,000 forged packets per second (about 4.5 Mbit/s) against a record with a 3,600-second TTL has about a 10 percent chance in 24 hours and 50 percent after a week; for a 60-second TTL, 10 percent after 24 minutes and 90 percent after about 9 hours. The TTL matters because the attacker can only race when the record is not already cached.

**The birthday attack (2002).** In the birthday paradox, 23 people are enough for an even chance that two share a birthday, because every pair is a chance to match. CERT/CC note VU#457875 (November 2002, crediting Vagner Sacramento of the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil) showed that some resolvers sent several identical queries for the same name at once if asked several times. Then each forged reply could match any of the $q$ outstanding queries, and the packets needed fell dramatically. RFC 5452's $D$ is exactly this count, and the fix was to never have more than one identical query outstanding.

blocks.code:
import math

def p_success(q, r, m):
    """q identical queries outstanding, r forged replies with distinct IDs,
    m possible ID values. Returns the chance at least one reply matches."""
    log_miss = sum(math.log1p(-q / (m - i)) for i in range(r))
    return 1 - math.exp(log_miss)

def replies_for_half(q, m):
    lo, hi = 1, m                      # binary search for the smallest r
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if p_success(q, mid, m) >= 0.5: hi = mid
        else: lo = mid + 1
    return lo

m = 2 ** 16                            # 16-bit query ID, fixed source port
for q in (1, 4, 200):
    r = replies_for_half(q, m)
    print(q, r, q + r)                 # total packets = queries + replies
# 1 32768 32769   |   4 10427 10431   |   200 227 427
best = min((q + replies_for_half(q, m), q) for q in range(1, 600))
print(best)                            # (426, 204): the cheapest mix
blocks.caption: Reproduces CERT VU#457875's table (32.7k, 10.4k, 427, and 426 packets for an unlimited number of queries). Runs in a few seconds.

blocks.title: Packets an attacker needs for a 50% chance (16-bit ID, fixed port)

scenes.caption: One outstanding query: the attacker must cover half of 65,536 IDs, 32,769 packets in total. This is the classic brute force.
Each extra identical query is another target every forged reply can hit. Four queries cut the cost to about a third.
With 200 identical queries outstanding, 427 packets give even odds: about 77 times cheaper. That is the birthday effect, and why resolvers now merge duplicate questions.

blocks.prompt: A resolver that once used one fixed source port now picks a random port from about 64,000 for each query. By roughly what factor does the attacker's work grow?
blocks.reveal: RFC 5452 says the problem space "expands by a factor of 64000": the attacker must now match port and ID together, so $P \approx 64{,}000$ in the formula. CERT's 2008 note describes the same change as "approximately 16 additional bits of randomness" ($2^{16} = 65{,}536$). The next lesson shows why this mattered so urgently in 2008.

blocks.question: Using RFC 5452's model, which change does NOT reduce an attacker's chance of poisoning a record?
options: Lowering the record's TTL so that wrong data expires sooner
Randomising the source port of each query
Raising the record's TTL
Never sending two identical queries at once
blocks.explain: A shorter TTL means the record leaves the cache more often, which gives the attacker more windows to race in (more attempts, T/TTL). Random ports grow the haystack, merging duplicates keeps D at 1, and a longer TTL means fewer windows.

blocks.question: Why does a forged reply need to arrive before the real one?
options: Because the first reply that passes the checks completes the query, and the real answer arriving later is dropped
Because the resolver checks timestamps
Because UDP delivers only one packet per port
Because the real server would detect the forgery
blocks.explain: Once a matching reply is accepted the query is no longer pending, so the later genuine reply has nothing to match and is discarded. The attacker is racing the real server, and only the attacker knows a race is happening.

blocks.md:
Recall from the prerequisite: in 2008 Dan Kaminsky, a researcher at the security firm IOActive, showed that cache poisoning was far more practical than believed (CERT/CC note VU#800113, 8 July 2008; CVE-2008-1447, where CVE is Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, the public catalogue of numbered flaws). This lesson takes the attack apart and puts numbers on it.

Before 2008, poisoning had a built-in speed limit. If `www.bank.example` was already cached, the attacker had to wait for its TTL to expire before racing again, so attempts were spaced minutes or hours apart. Kaminsky found a way around the wait, and a way to make one win far more valuable. The emergency patches randomised source ports.

**Trick 1: names that are never cached.** As Friedl's guide explains, the attacker asks the resolver for a random name such as `www12345678.bank.example`, which cannot be in the cache. The resolver must ask the real server, which opens a fresh race window. If the attacker loses, they ask for `www12345679.bank.example` and race again at once. There is no TTL to wait for: in RFC 5452's terms the effective TTL becomes the window itself.

**Trick 2: forge the delegation, not the answer.** Instead of a fake address for one random name, the forged reply says "I do not know, ask these name servers", an **authority** (NS) record for `bank.example`, plus **glue** records (the addresses of those name servers) pointing at the attacker. These records are in the same domain as the question, so bailiwick checking accepts them. One match and the resolver believes the attacker runs the entire zone. Friedl notes the forger also sets a very high TTL so the poison stays.

blocks.title: One round of the Kaminsky race

scenes.caption: The attacker (any client the resolver serves, or a web page that makes a browser look names up) asks for a random, uncached name.
The resolver sends its own query to the real name server, with a query ID and source port the attacker cannot see.
The attacker floods forged replies, each guessing an ID (and port). Their content: 'ask ns.bank.example, which is at the attacker's IP'.
Usually the real answer wins and the forgeries are discarded. Nothing is lost: the attacker simply starts again with a new random name.
Eventually one guess matches first. The resolver caches the attacker's servers as authoritative for all of bank.example, with a long TTL.

blocks.md: **How fast?** RFC 5452 works this case out. With the same 7,000 forged packets per second and a single source port, the chance "rises to 50% within 7 seconds". With 64,000 random ports, the same rate needs "around 116 hours". The plot uses that model with one authoritative server: a fresh name every window means the window length cancels out, leaving $P(T) = 1 - e^{-T R / (P \cdot 65536)}$. Drag the rate slider: even a far larger attacker stays slow against random ports, which is why source port randomisation was the emergency patch.

blocks.title: Chance of poisoning over time, with uncached random names

scenes.caption: Simplified model from RFC 5452 section 8.1. With one source port, 7,000 forged packets per second reach even odds in about 6.5 seconds (the RFC rounds to 7).
Random ports multiply the haystack by 64,000. The same attacker needs about 415,000 seconds, roughly 115 hours, and that much spoofed traffic is easy to notice.
A 14 times bigger attacker (100,000 packets per second) still needs about 8 hours against random ports. Randomisation buys time and visibility, not certainty.

blocks.title: Time to a 50% chance, log10 of seconds (7,000 forged packets/s)

scenes.caption: Each cell is log10 of the seconds to even odds, for one authoritative server. The TTL figures quoted in lesson 5 use RFC 5452's typical 2.5 servers, so they are 2.5 times longer. 0.8 is about 6 s, 5.6 about 4.8 days, 10.2 about 500 years.
Top row: Kaminsky's random names remove the TTL wait, so even 2,048 ports (Friedl's rounding of the 2,500 ports Microsoft's patched server was said to use) fall in about 3.7 hours.
Right column: with 64,000 random ports every scenario is days or longer. Bottom row: long TTLs helped only while attackers had to wait for expiry.

blocks.md: **Defender's view in 2008 and now.** CERT's advice: patch resolvers to randomise source ports; restrict recursion to your own clients (an open resolver answers anyone); filter spoofed packets at the network edge (BCP 38); and watch for traffic NAT devices may un-randomise, because port address translation can rewrite random source ports into predictable ones. Signals in resolver logs: bursts of queries for many random names under one domain, and floods of replies with wrong query IDs. Friedl adds that a resolver need not be internet-facing to be attacked: a web page can make browsers inside the network trigger the lookups.

Kaminsky's insight was economic: random names make every attempt immediately repeatable, and forged delegations make one success worth a whole domain. The fix multiplied the guessing space by about 64,000; only signed data (DNSSEC, next lesson) removes the guessing game entirely.

blocks.question: Why did Kaminsky's attack use names like www12345678.bank.example instead of www.bank.example?
options: A name that is not cached forces a new query to the real server at once, so the attacker can race again immediately instead of waiting for a TTL
Random names are shorter, so forged packets are smaller
Random names bypass bailiwick checking
Resolvers do not check query IDs for random names
blocks.explain: The whole speed-up comes from always asking for an uncached name. Each one opens a fresh window, so attempts are limited only by how fast the attacker can send, not by record TTLs.

blocks.question: A company patched its resolver to randomise source ports in 2008, but its firewall performs port address translation on outgoing DNS and assigns ports sequentially. What is the effect?
options: The firewall makes the outgoing ports predictable again, undoing much of the patch
DNS stops working
None: the resolver's randomness survives translation
The firewall blocks all forged replies
blocks.explain: CERT's note warns that port address translation (PAT) devices rewrite source ports and 'can reduce or eliminate improvements gained by patching DNS software'. The attacker sees the translated port, so predictable translation hands back the 16 bits the patch added.

lessons.title: DNSSEC, encrypted DNS, and DNS tunnelling as a signal

blocks.md:
Random ports make forgery expensive. **DNSSEC** (DNS Security Extensions, RFC 4033) makes it pointless: zone owners sign their records, and a validating resolver rejects anything whose signature does not check, however well the attacker guessed the ID. The extensions "provide origin authentication and integrity assurance services for DNS data" through four new record types:

- **DNSKEY**: a zone's public key.
- **RRSIG** (Resource Record Signature): a signature over a set of records.
- **DS** (Delegation Signer): placed in the *parent* zone, a hash of the child zone's key, which links parent to child.
- **NSEC** (Next Secure): signed proof that a name does not exist, so "no such name" cannot be forged either.

blocks.title: The DNSSEC chain of trust for www.example.

nodes.label:
Root zone
DNSKEY + DS for example.

scenes.caption: A validating resolver starts from a trust anchor: a key it was configured with outside DNS (RFC 4033).
The root's key verifies the root's records, including a DS record holding a hash of example.'s key.
The resolver fetches example.'s DNSKEY and checks its hash against the DS. A match extends trust one level down.
example.'s key verifies the RRSIG over the www address record. The answer is authentic.
A forged reply, even with the right query ID, carries no signature made with example.'s private key. Validation fails and the resolver returns an error instead of the lie.

blocks.md:
**What DNSSEC does not do**, in RFC 4033's own words: it is "not designed to provide confidentiality" (queries and answers are still readable), and it "provides no protection against denial of service attacks". It also only helps where the zone is signed *and* the resolver validates. In the 2018 MyEtherWallet case (lesson 8), Cloudflare noted that signed records would have exposed the fake answers.

**Encrypted transport** solves a different problem: who can read or alter DNS between your device and your resolver.
- **DoT**, DNS over TLS ([RFC 7858](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7858)), runs DNS inside TLS on TCP port **853**.
- **DoH**, DNS over HTTPS ([RFC 8484](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8484)), sends DNS messages as HTTPS requests (GET or POST, media type `application/dns-message`), on port 443 like other web traffic. DNS over QUIC (RFC 9250) is a newer option.

Both stop an on-path attacker (an ARP spoofer, a hostile Wi-Fi) from reading or forging your lookups. Neither authenticates the data itself, and the resolver you chose still sees every name.

Defender's trade-off: encrypted DNS removes a signal security teams relied on (plaintext DNS on port 53). The usual answer is to point managed devices at the organisation's own resolver over DoT or DoH and log there, and to treat DNS traffic to unexpected outside resolvers as worth investigating.

**DNS tunnelling.** Because DNS is allowed almost everywhere, attackers hide data in it. MITRE ATT&CK (a public catalogue of attacker techniques run by the non-profit MITRE) lists it as technique T1071.004: "Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic". The pattern: malware encodes stolen data into the leftmost label of a name under a domain the attacker controls, for example `mzxw6ytboi2dcmrtgq3tmnzy.t.example.net`. The resolver dutifully forwards it to the attacker's authoritative server, which decodes the label and answers with commands, often in TXT records.

MITRE's suggested detections: "high volume, long subdomain lengths, encoded payload patterns", queries from processes that do not normally do DNS, and infrequent but regular beacons.

blocks.caption: Illustrative dns.log lines from Zeek (an open-source network monitor that turns traffic into logs; lessons 14 and 17 cover it) (JSON format; field names from Zeek's documentation, values invented). Note the 60-second spacing, the TXT type, and the long random-looking first label under one domain.
Two classic features: length of the first label and its character entropy. Real detections combine them with volume per domain and per host, because CDNs also use long, random-looking names.

blocks.title: First-label length and entropy: normal names vs a tunnel

scenes.caption: Length of the leftmost label in characters. Ordinary hostnames are short words; tunnel labels are packed with encoded data (24 characters here, and often far longer).
Entropy in bits per character, computed by the script above. Encoded data looks random (3.5 to 4.0 here); words repeat letters.

blocks.code: alert dns $HOME_NET any -> any any (msg:"Possible DNS tunnelling: very long query name"; dns.query; bsize:>60; threshold: type both, track by_src, count 20, seconds 300; classtype:policy-violation; sid:1000101; rev:1;)
blocks.caption: A rule for Suricata (an open-source intrusion detection engine, covered in lesson 17; keywords dns.query, bsize and threshold from Suricata's documentation): alert once per source when a host sends 20 or more queries longer than 60 bytes within five minutes. Thresholds need tuning per network.

blocks.question: A site's zone is DNSSEC-signed and your resolver validates. An attacker on the café Wi-Fi can read your DNS traffic. Which is true?
options: DNSSEC hides your queries from the attacker
Nothing is protected without DoH
The attacker can forge answers as long as the query ID matches
The attacker can read which names you look up but cannot get a forged answer accepted for that signed zone
blocks.explain: DNSSEC gives integrity and origin authentication, not confidentiality. Forged answers fail validation, but the questions are still visible. Hiding them is the job of DoT or DoH between you and the resolver.

blocks.question: Which pattern in DNS logs most suggests tunnelling rather than normal browsing?
options: Many A queries for popular sites during working hours
Queries for the company's own domain
A few NXDOMAIN answers for typos
One host sending a steady stream of TXT queries with long, high-entropy first labels under the same unfamiliar domain
blocks.explain: Tunnels need many queries to move data, under one domain the attacker controls, with encoded labels, often using TXT records for replies. Ordinary browsing is spread over many domains with short, word-like labels.

lessons.title: BGP hijacks and route leaks: the MyEtherWallet case

blocks.md:
Recall from the prerequisite: networks called **autonomous systems** (ASes, each with a number such as AS16509) tell each other which address blocks (prefixes) they can reach using **BGP** (Border Gateway Protocol), and routers prefer the most specific matching prefix. Nothing in BGP itself checks that an AS is entitled to announce what it announces.

Two kinds of incident follow:
- A **hijack**: an AS announces a prefix it does not hold, either the same prefix as the owner or a more specific one (which wins everywhere it is accepted, as YouTube learned in 2008).
- A **route leak**, defined by [RFC 7908](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7908) as "the propagation of routing announcement(s) beyond their intended scope", for example a customer passing routes it learned from one provider to another provider. RFC 9234 notes leaks "are usually the result of misconfigured or absent BGP route filtering".

The Pakistan Telecom case was both: a hijack meant for domestic use that leaked to the world.

**Case: Amazon Route 53 and MyEtherWallet, 24 April 2018.** Louis Poinsignon of Cloudflare reconstructed it from Cloudflare's route collectors. Between about 11:05 and 12:55 UTC (other monitors saw it until 13:03), eNet Inc (AS10297), a provider in Columbus, Ohio, announced five /24 prefixes inside Amazon's (AS16509) address space, such as `205.251.192.0/24`, and Hurricane Electric (AS6939), a large transit network that eNet forwarded them to, passed them on. Those addresses belong to **Route 53**, Amazon's authoritative DNS service.

Any resolver whose network accepted the route sent its Route 53 questions to the attacker's server. That server answered only for `myetherwallet.com`, a web wallet for the Ethereum cryptocurrency, with addresses at a Russian hosting provider; other names got errors (SERVFAIL). Cloudflare's own public resolver 1.1.1.1 was poisoned in cities including Chicago, Sydney and Manila. Users did not need to accept the bad route themselves, only to use a resolver that had.

blocks.title: Route 53 hijack: routing, then DNS, then the browser

scenes.caption: Normally resolvers reach Route 53's name servers at Amazon, which answer for thousands of customer domains.
11:05 UTC: eNet announces more-specific /24s of Route 53's space; Hurricane Electric propagates them. Where accepted, they beat Amazon's routes.
Those resolvers now send Route 53 questions to the impostor. It answers myetherwallet.com with an attacker IP and caches it in the resolver.
Users of those resolvers reach the phishing copy. Its certificate was self-signed, so browsers warned. Users who clicked through sent their credentials; the attacker used them to take Ethereum.

blocks.md:
**Defender's view.** Three layers each could have stopped it, as Cloudflare's write-up concludes:

1. **Routing:** the other providers eNet used (CenturyLink, Cogent and NTT) did not seem to accept the route, which Cloudflare attributes possibly to filters. Filtering customer announcements against registry data, and RPKI (next lesson), stop most such routes.
2. **DNS:** had the zone been DNSSEC-signed and resolvers validating, the forged answers would have failed.
3. **TLS:** the browser warning was correct. With HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security, a header with which a site tells browsers to reach it only over HTTPS and, per RFC 6797, to fail certificate errors with "no user recourse"), browsers that already held the policy from an earlier visit or a built-in preload list would have refused to continue.

**Detection:** routing changes are public. Route collectors (Cloudflare's, RIPE NCC's RIS) record every announcement, so an operator can alert within minutes when anyone else originates, or announces more specifics of, their prefixes.

A BGP hijack does not need to touch your servers or your users' networks. It moves traffic somewhere else on the internet, where your TLS certificate, DNSSEC signatures and user training are the remaining defences.

blocks.question: An AS announces 205.251.192.0/24 while the owner announces 205.251.192.0/23. Where accepted, which wins, and why?
options: The /24, because routers choose the longest (most specific) matching prefix
Neither: routers drop overlapping prefixes
Whichever has the shorter AS path
The /23, because it was announced first
blocks.explain: Longest prefix match is applied before any BGP preference between routes: a /24 is more specific than a /23, so destinations inside it follow the /24. AS path length only decides between announcements of the same prefix.

blocks.question: MyEtherWallet users who used a resolver whose network had NOT accepted the bad route were...
options: Affected because Route 53 was offline everywhere
Not affected: their resolver still reached Amazon's real name servers
Affected only if they used DNS over HTTPS
Also affected, because the hijack changed the domain's registration
blocks.explain: The hijack only diverted traffic in networks that accepted the more-specific routes. Cloudflare saw 1.1.1.1 poisoned in some cities and working normally in the rest of the world, which is why the impact had a geography.

blocks.md:
The fix for "anyone can announce anything" is to let address holders publish, in a verifiable way, who may announce their addresses. That system is the **RPKI** (Resource Public Key Infrastructure, RFC 6480): a hierarchy of certificates, rooted in the regional internet registries that hand out addresses, attesting who holds which IP blocks and AS numbers.

The holder then signs a **ROA** (Route Origin Authorization): "an explicit authorization by an address holder that a given AS is permitted to originate routes to a set of addresses". A ROA names a prefix, an origin AS, and a **maxLength**, the longest (most specific) prefix length that AS may announce within it.

**Route origin validation** (ROV, RFC 6811) is what routers do with ROAs. Validators download and check the signed objects and give routers a list of **VRPs** (Validated ROA Payloads: prefix, max length, origin AS). For each route the router asks two questions, using RFC 6811's terms:

- Is the route's prefix **covered** by a VRP (equal to it or more specific)?
- Is it **matched**: covered, prefix length no more than the VRP's maxLength, and the route's origin AS (the last AS in its path) equal to the VRP's AS?

The result is one of three states: **Valid** (at least one VRP matches), **Invalid** (some VRP covers it but none matches) or **NotFound** (no VRP covers it). Networks doing ROV typically drop Invalid routes; RFC 6811 leaves that as local policy.

blocks.title: Route origin validation, step by step (RFC 6811 logic)
blocks.code:
import ipaddress as ip

# Illustrative VRPs, as if the holders had published ROAs.
VRPS = [
    (ip.ip_network("205.251.192.0/21"), 21, 16509),   # prefix, maxLength, AS
    (ip.ip_network("208.65.152.0/22"), 24, 36561),
]

def validate(prefix, origin_as):
    route = ip.ip_network(prefix)
    covered = False
    for vrp, max_len, vrp_as in VRPS:
        if route.subnet_of(vrp):                   # covered
            covered = True
            if route.prefixlen <= max_len and origin_as == vrp_as:
                return "Valid"                     # matched
    return "Invalid" if covered else "NotFound"

print(validate("205.251.192.0/21", 16509))   # the owner
print(validate("205.251.192.0/24", 10297))   # 2018-style hijack
print(validate("208.65.153.0/24", 17557))    # 2008-style hijack
print(validate("208.65.153.0/24", 36561))    # owner, within maxLength
print(validate("198.51.100.0/24", 64500))    # no ROA at all

scenes.caption: Two illustrative VRPs. These are not real ROAs from the 2008 or 2018 incidents; they show what such records would have done.
The owner's own /21 from AS16509: covered by the first VRP, length 21 within maxLength 21, origin matches.
A /24 from AS10297: covered (inside the /21), but too specific for maxLength 21 and from the wrong AS. Covered but not matched means Invalid.
Pakistan Telecom's 2008 /24 from AS17557: covered by YouTube's VRP, wrong origin AS. Invalid, and dropped by any network doing ROV.
The same /24 from YouTube's own AS is Valid because maxLength 24 allows it, so the owner could have answered with a /24 of its own.
No VRP covers this prefix, so ROV has no opinion: NotFound. Most routes on the internet were in this state before ROAs became common.

blocks.md:
**Limits, stated by RFC 6811 itself.** ROV checks only the *origin*. An attacker can "prepend the 'valid' source AS to a forged BGP route announcement", making a fake path that ends in the right AS. It "does not protect against 'AS-in-the-middle attacks' or provide any path validation" and "should be thought of more as a protection against misconfiguration than as true 'security' in the strong sense". That is still a great deal: most famous incidents, including both cases above, were wrong-origin announcements.

Two practical rules follow. Set maxLength no longer than the prefixes you really announce (a generous maxLength lets a forged-origin attacker announce a more specific that still validates); RFC 9319, a 2022 Best Current Practice, says operators "SHOULD avoid using the maxLength attribute" unless they need it. And remember ROV protects only through the networks that do it; Cloudflare's [Is BGP safe yet?](https://isbgpsafeyet.com/) page tests whether your own provider drops Invalid routes.

**Route leaks need a different tool**, because a leaked route usually has the correct origin. RFC 9234 (2022) has neighbours agree on their relationship in the BGP OPEN message (provider, customer, peer, and so on) and adds an **OTC** (Only to Customer) attribute, so that routes are marked, "allowing both prevention and detection of route leaks". MANRS (Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security), an industry initiative, asks operators for the basics: filter customer announcements, prevent spoofed source addresses, coordinate, and publish routing data such as ROAs. For paths, the IETF is standardising ASPA (Autonomous System Provider Authorization): signed lists of each AS's upstream providers, which let routers spot leaks and forged paths. As of late 2026 it is still an Internet-Draft.

RPKI answers 'may this AS originate this prefix?'. It turns the most common hijack, a wrong origin or an unexpected more specific, into an Invalid route that validating networks drop. It does not validate paths or stop leaks with the correct origin.

blocks.question: A ROA says 203.0.113.0/24, maxLength 24, AS64500. A route for 203.0.113.0/25 arrives with origin AS64500. What is its ROV state?
options: Valid, because the origin AS matches
Valid, because /25 is inside /24
NotFound, because no ROA has exactly that prefix
Invalid, because the /25 is covered by the ROA but longer than its maxLength
blocks.explain: Covered (the /25 is inside the /24) but not matched, since 25 exceeds maxLength 24. Covered and not matched is Invalid, even with the right origin. This stops anyone, including a misconfigured owner, from announcing unexpected more specifics.

blocks.question: Why does RFC 6811 call origin validation mainly protection against misconfiguration?
options: Because a deliberate attacker can forge a path ending in the authorised origin AS, which ROV accepts
Because ROAs are unsigned
Because ROV only works for IPv6
Because routers ignore Invalid routes by default
blocks.explain: ROV checks the last AS in the path and nothing else. A careful attacker appends the legitimate origin to their announcement. Accidental hijacks, such as the 2008 YouTube event, carry the wrong origin and are caught.

blocks.md:
Recall the TCP three-way handshake: the client sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK and waits, the client finishes with ACK. While it waits, the server holds a record of the half-open connection, part of what RFC 9293 calls a TCB (Transmission Control Block). A **SYN flood** fills the space for those records.

Tiny example: a server keeps at most 4 half-open connections per listening port and forgets one after 75 seconds without an ACK. Four forged SYNs every 75 seconds keep it full, and every real client is turned away.

**History**, from RFC 4987 ("TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations", 2007): the weakness "was discovered as early as 1994 by Bill Cheswick and Steve Bellovin", who removed a paragraph about it from their book on firewalls. It was publicised in 1996 in Phrack Magazine, an online hacker magazine, with working code, and by September 1996 an attack on an ISP's mail servers "caused well-publicized outages"; CERT issued advisory CA-96.21. It was serious because it "targets end-host resources, which require fewer packets to deplete".

**Mechanism:** send SYNs, usually from spoofed source addresses that will never answer the SYN-ACK, fast enough to keep the **backlog** (the queue of half-open connections for a port) full. RFC 4987 notes typical defaults then were "a half-dozen to several dozen" entries, with timers such as 75 seconds before an entry is reclaimed. Linux's `tcp_max_syn_backlog` is at least 128 and grows with memory.

blocks.title: A 4-slot backlog held full by forged SYNs (toy numbers)

scenes.caption: Simplified: 4 slots, 75-second timeout. At t=0 four forged SYNs arrive. The server answers each to a spoofed address that never replies.
At t=30 a real client sends SYN. Every slot is taken, so it is dropped. It retries, and is dropped again.
At t=75 slots expire, and the attacker refills them at once. Four packets per 75 seconds hold the port shut: the attack needs almost no bandwidth.

blocks.md:
Scale the toy up: holding a 128-entry backlog with a 75-second timer needs only about 128 / 75, or 1.7 SYNs per second. Bigger backlogs and shorter timers help a little (RFC 4987 discusses both), but the real fix removes the state altogether.

**SYN cookies** (the idea is credited to the cryptographer Daniel J. Bernstein; RFC 4987 points to Bernstein's site as the best reference) "allocate no state at all" for half-open connections. The server encodes what it needs into the initial sequence number of its SYN-ACK. RFC 4987's appendix describes one layout of the 32 bits: the top 5 bits from a counter that ticks every 64 seconds, 3 bits for one of 8 common MSS values (Maximum Segment Size, the largest chunk the client accepts), and 24 bits from a secret function of the addresses, ports and counter. A real client's ACK echoes that number plus one, so the server can recompute and check it, then create the connection.

blocks.title: Making and checking a SYN cookie (simplified from RFC 4987)
blocks.code:
import hmac, hashlib, time

SECRET = b"server-secret-rotated-regularly"
MSS_TABLE = [536, 1220, 1440, 1460, 4312, 8960, 9000, 65495]

def mac24(src, sport, dst, dport, t):
    msg = f"{src}:{sport}>{dst}:{dport}@{t}".encode()
    d = hmac.new(SECRET, msg, hashlib.sha256).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(d[:3], "big")             # 24 bits

def make_cookie(src, sport, dst, dport, client_isn, mss):
    t = int(time.time()) // 64 % 32                  # 5-bit counter
    idx = max(i for i, m in enumerate(MSS_TABLE) if m <= mss)
    raw = (t << 27) | (idx << 24) | mac24(src, sport, dst, dport, t)
    return raw ^ client_isn                          # SYN-ACK sequence number

def check_ack(src, sport, dst, dport, client_isn, ack_no):
    raw = ((ack_no - 1) % 2**32) ^ client_isn
    t, idx = raw >> 27, (raw >> 24) & 7
    now = int(time.time()) // 64 % 32
    if t not in (now, (now - 1) % 32):               # too old: reject
        return None
    if raw & 0xFFFFFF != mac24(src, sport, dst, dport, t):
        return None                                  # forged or guessed
    return MSS_TABLE[idx]                            # accept, with this MSS

scenes.caption: A SYN arrives. Instead of storing anything, the server computes a cookie from the connection's addresses and a secret.
Top 5 bits: time counter. Next 3: MSS index. Low 24: keyed hash. RFC 4987 also XORs in the client's own ISN. This number becomes the SYN-ACK's sequence number; no state is kept.
Only a client that really received the SYN-ACK can send ACK = cookie + 1. The server undoes the XOR and splits the fields.
Old counters are rejected (a cookie is valid for about two minutes), then the hash is recomputed. A spoofed SYN never produces an ACK, so it costs the server nothing.

blocks.md:
**The price.** Only a few bits fit, so options such as window scaling may be lost; RFC 4987 calls disabling it "the largest price". Linux therefore uses cookies as a fallback: its `tcp_syncookies` [setting](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/ip-sysctl.html) defaults to 1, meaning "send out syncookies when the syn backlog queue of a socket overflows", and the kernel documentation warns that cookies "MUST NOT be used to help highly loaded servers" cope with legitimate load.

**Defender's view.** On the host: a large and growing count of connections in SYN-RECV state, and kernel log warnings about possible SYN flooding. On the network: many SYNs to one destination port from many sources, with the handshake never completed. In Zeek's `conn.log`, whose history field uses upper case for the originator and lower case for the responder, such connections show `Sh` (SYN, then the server's SYN-ACK) and never the client's ACK. Mirai's attacks on Dyn in 2016 (lesson 13) were largely SYN floods on DNS port 53.

blocks.code:
# Linux: check the setting (1 = cookies when the backlog overflows)
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies
# Count half-open connections right now
ss -Hn state syn-recv | wc -l

# Suricata: many SYNs to one of our hosts in a short time (tune count and seconds)
alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"Possible SYN flood"; flow:stateless; flags:S,12; threshold: type both, track by_dst, count 5000, seconds 10; classtype:attempted-dos; sid:1000102; rev:1;)
blocks.caption: Run the first two on your own Linux machine. The rule's flags:S,12 matches SYN without ACK, ignoring the two bits used by ECN, Explicit Congestion Notification (CWR and ECE), as in Suricata's documentation examples.

blocks.md: A SYN flood attacks memory, not bandwidth: a few packets per second can hold a backlog full. SYN cookies move the half-open state into the sequence number the client must echo, so spoofed SYNs cost the server almost nothing.

blocks.question: Why do SYN floods usually use spoofed source addresses, and why does that matter for SYN cookies?
options: Spoofed sources never send the final ACK, so their entries sit in the backlog; with cookies there is no entry, and no ACK means no work
Spoofing makes packets smaller; cookies need small packets
Spoofed addresses bypass the firewall; cookies re-enable it
Spoofing is required by TCP; cookies remove the requirement
blocks.explain: The flood works because each SYN creates state that waits for an ACK that never comes. SYN cookies create no state, and the only thing that creates a connection is a correct ACK, which a spoofing attacker never sees the SYN-ACK to compute.

blocks.question: A server enables SYN cookies permanently (Linux setting 2) to improve performance under normal heavy load. What does the kernel documentation say about this?
options: It disables the three-way handshake
It has no side effects
It is wrong: cookies are a fallback; they lose TCP extensions and can degrade service, so tune the backlog for real load instead
It is the recommended setting for busy servers
blocks.explain: The documentation says syncookies must not be used to help highly loaded servers handle legal connection rates, because they do not allow TCP extensions. Setting 2 exists to test their effect, not as a tuning knob.

lessons.title: RST injection and the history of TCP session hijacking

blocks.md:
SYN floods stop new connections. Other attacks target connections that already exist. RFC 5961 (2010) lists what an off-path attacker can inject into someone else's TCP connection if it can make the receiver accept a forged segment: a **RST** to tear the connection down, a **SYN** to make the receiver think its peer restarted, or **data** to corrupt the stream.

To be accepted the forged segment needs the right 4-tuple (both addresses and ports) and, under the original 1981 TCP rules, a sequence number anywhere inside the receiver's current **window** (the range of byte numbers it is ready to accept). RFC 5961 points out that long-lived connections with predictable ports, its example being BGP sessions between routers, make the 4-tuple easy to guess.

**The arithmetic.** Sequence numbers are 32 bits, about 4.29 billion values. If any value inside a 65,535-byte window is accepted, the attacker steps through the space one window at a time: $2^{32} / 65{,}535 \approx 65{,}537$ forged RSTs cover every possibility (half that on average). At 10,000 packets per second that is under 7 seconds. RFC 5961 notes default windows of "32,768 or 65,535 depending upon the operating system", and bigger windows make the attack cheaper.

**The fix (RFC 5961 section 3).** Reset only if the sequence number *exactly* equals the next expected one. If it is merely inside the window, send a **challenge ACK** stating the real expected number and drop the segment. A real peer that did mean to reset replies with an exact RST; a blind attacker never sees the challenge. The attacker now needs the exact value: $2^{31}$ tries on average, about 2.5 days at the same rate. SYNs arriving on an open connection get the same challenge treatment.

blocks.title: Forged RSTs needed to cover the sequence space

scenes.caption: Old rules: one forged RST per window-sized step. A 65,535-byte window needs about 65,537 packets to cover all 2^32 numbers, and larger windows need fewer.
RFC 5961: only an exact match resets; in-window guesses get a challenge ACK. The space to cover is the full 2^32 whatever the window size.

blocks.title: A blind RST meets a challenge ACK

scenes.caption: Routers A and B hold a long-lived BGP session over TCP. B next expects sequence number 5,000,000 from A.
The attacker spoofs A's address and sends RSTs with guessed sequence numbers. Most land outside the window and are silently dropped.
One guess lands inside the window but is not exact. Old TCP would tear the session down here.
RFC 5961 behaviour: B sends a challenge ACK to the real A, saying 'I expect 5,000,000', and drops the RST.
A never sent a RST, so it simply carries on. The session survives, and the attacker never saw the challenge.

blocks.md:
**Session hijacking, the history.** Forging a whole connection requires predicting the server's initial sequence number (ISN), which the client must acknowledge without seeing. RFC 6528 (2012) recounts it: in 1985 Robert Morris described, in the AT&T Bell Laboratories report "A Weakness in the 4.2BSD UNIX TCP/IP Software", an attack in which "the attacker gags a host trusted by the target, impersonates the IP address of the trusted host" and "completes the three-way handshake based on its guess at the next ISN". Combined with address-based trust (the old Unix `rsh` commands accepted logins because of the source IP alone), that let attackers run commands. Its "exploitation was widely publicized about 10 years later", in 1995, when Tsutomu Shimomura, a security researcher, posted technical details of such an attack to the USENET discussion system.

The root cause was the ISN generator in the original TCP specification: a global counter "incremented by 1 roughly every 4 microseconds", trivial to predict after one probe connection.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, os, time

SECRET = os.urandom(16)          # chosen at boot, never revealed

def isn(local_ip, local_port, remote_ip, remote_port):
    """RFC 6528: ISN = M + F(4-tuple, secret key).
    M is a 4-microsecond timer, so numbers still increase over time;
    F is a keyed hash, so each connection's numbers start somewhere secret."""
    m = int(time.monotonic() * 1_000_000) // 4
    f = hashlib.sha256(f"{local_ip}{local_port}{remote_ip}{remote_port}".encode()
                       + SECRET).digest()
    return (m + int.from_bytes(f[:4], "big")) % 2**32

print(isn("192.0.2.10", 22, "198.51.100.7", 50001))
print(isn("192.0.2.10", 22, "198.51.100.7", 50002))  # unrelated value
blocks.caption: RFC 6528's design, simplified (it suggests a hash such as MD5 of the 4-tuple and key; SHA-256 here). Learning the ISN of your own connection tells you nothing about another 4-tuple's.

blocks.md:
**What is left today.** Off-path guessing is hard thanks to random ISNs, random client ports and RFC 5961. An *on-path* attacker needs no guessing at all: it sees the numbers and can inject or reset at will. RFC 6528 states plainly that "the proper solution for these attacks is cryptographic authentication". TLS and SSH protect the *content*: injected data fails their integrity check. But they run on top of TCP and cannot authenticate TCP's own control bits, so a forged RST can still end a TLS connection. Long-lived router sessions therefore use TCP-level options that authenticate segments (RFC 5961 mentions TCP MD5 signatures, RFC 2385, since replaced by TCP-AO, the TCP Authentication Option, RFC 5925). Even the fix needed a fix: Linux capped challenge ACKs with one global counter, which let an off-path attacker infer and hijack connections (CVE-2016-5696, fixed in Linux 4.7).

**Defender's view:** bursts of RSTs or challenge ACKs, BGP sessions flapping for no operational reason, and router counters for TCP segments with bad sequence numbers.

Address-based trust is the real bug behind classic hijacking. Any system that grants access because a packet claims a source IP (old rsh, IP allow lists alone, zone transfers allowed by address) is relying on something an attacker can forge. Use cryptographic authentication.

blocks.question: Under the original TCP rules, an off-path attacker targets a session with a 65,535-byte window. Roughly how many forged RSTs are needed to be sure of hitting the window?
options: 65,535 squared
Exactly 1, if the 4-tuple is right
About 65,537
2^32, about 4.3 billion
blocks.explain: Any value inside the window is accepted, so stepping by the window size covers the 2^32 space in 2^32 / 65,535, about 65,537 packets. RFC 5961's exact-match rule removes the window from the equation, restoring the full 2^32 space.

blocks.question: A company runs SSH everywhere. An attacker gets on-path between two servers. Which attack still works?
options: Tearing the connection down with a forged TCP RST
Reading the SSH session's commands
Injecting commands into the SSH stream
Predicting the SSH host key
blocks.explain: SSH encrypts and authenticates its stream, so reading and injection fail. TCP's control bits sit below SSH and are not authenticated, and an on-path attacker sees the exact sequence numbers, so a forged RST still resets the connection.

lessons.title: DDoS: three classes, and the maths of amplification

blocks.md:
A **denial of service** (DoS) attack makes a service unavailable to its real users; a **distributed** one (DDoS) uses many machines, often a botnet. Engineers sort floods by the resource they exhaust:

- **Volumetric:** fill the network links with more bits than they carry (UDP floods, reflection and amplification).
- **Protocol, or state exhaustion:** use up tables kept by servers, firewalls or load balancers (SYN floods, ACK floods).
- **Application layer:** send requests that are expensive to answer (HTTP floods), usually small and hard to tell from real users.

The Mirai botnet study by Antonakakis and colleagues (USENIX Security 2017) classified the 15,194 attack commands Mirai's operators issued between September 2016 and February 2017 exactly this way and found the three classes "equally prevalent".

blocks.title: Mirai's 15,194 attack commands by class (USENIX Security 2017)

scenes.caption: Application-layer commands in the paper's Table 9: HTTP, DNS, GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation, a tunnelling protocol) and VSE floods, which the paper ties to Valve's Steam game servers. 5,274 in total.
Volumetric (UDP and plain UDP floods): 4,982. TCP state exhaustion (SYN, ACK and ACK-STOMP floods): 4,938. Sums computed from the paper's Table 9.

blocks.md:
**Reflection and amplification.** Recall from the prerequisite: a UDP request is a complete transaction, so an attacker can forge the victim's address as the source and the server (the **reflector**) sends its answer to the victim. If the answer is much bigger than the question, the reflector is also an **amplifier**.

CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency), crediting researcher Christian Rossow, measures this with the **bandwidth amplification factor** (BAF): "the number of UDP payload bytes that an amplifier sends to answer a request, compared to the number of UDP payload bytes of the request".

blocks.tex: \text{BAF} = \frac{\text{response payload bytes}}{\text{request payload bytes}} \qquad \text{attacker bandwidth} = \frac{\text{bandwidth at victim}}{\text{BAF}}
blocks.caption: The second formula is the attacker's economics: divide the flood you want by the BAF to get the spoofed traffic you must send.

blocks.code:
def baf(request_bytes, response_bytes):
    return response_bytes / request_bytes

# Cloudflare's memcached measurement: a 15-byte request, a 750 kB answer
print(baf(15, 750 * 1024))                    # 51200.0

target_bps = 1.35e12                          # GitHub's 2018 peak, bits/s
for name, factor in [("DNS", 54), ("SSDP", 30.8), ("CharGEN", 358.8),
                     ("NTP", 556.9), ("memcached", 51200)]:
    print(f"{name:10s} needs {target_bps / factor / 1e9:8.3f} Gbit/s of spoofed requests")
# abbreviated: DNS 25.000 | SSDP 43.831 | CharGEN 3.763 | NTP 2.424 | memcached 0.026

print(1.35e12 / 8 / 126.9e6)                  # about 1330 bytes per packet
blocks.caption: BAF values from CISA's table (DNS up to 54; SSDP, Simple Service Discovery Protocol, 30.8; CharGEN, Character Generator Protocol, 358.8; NTP, Network Time Protocol, 556.9) and Cloudflare's memcached figure (it counts 750 kB as 768,000 bytes). The last line uses GitHub's reported peak rates.

blocks.title: Spoofed traffic needed for a 1.35 Tbps flood, by reflector

scenes.caption: Even DNS, the classic amplifier, needs 25 Gbit/s of spoofed queries to produce 1.35 Tbps at the victim.
NTP and CharGEN cut that to a few Gbit/s. memcached needs about 26 Mbit/s, roughly one home connection's upload. That is why the 2018 attacks were sudden and huge.

blocks.md: **Case: GitHub, 28 February 2018, from the defender's chair.** GitHub's incident report: at 17:21 UTC monitoring "detected an anomaly in the ratio of ingress to egress traffic" (far more bytes coming in than going out, the opposite of a web service's normal shape). Inbound transit passed 100 Gbps in one facility, so at 17:26 engineers withdrew GitHub's BGP announcements from its transit providers and announced its network (AS36459) only through Akamai, a provider with far more edge capacity, whose access control lists dropped the attack. Full recovery was reported at 17:30. The attack "originated from over a thousand different autonomous systems (ASNs) across tens of thousands of unique endpoints" and peaked at 1.35 Tbps and 126.9 million packets per second, about 1,330 bytes per packet: large reflected responses, not small requests.

blocks.title: GitHub, 28 February 2018 (minutes after 17:00 UTC)

scenes.caption: 17:21: the flood arrives. Monitoring flags the ingress to egress ratio and pages the on-call engineer. The site is unavailable.
17:26: GitHub announces its prefixes only via Akamai, which scrubs the attack at its edge. Service is intermittent while routes converge.
17:30: full recovery. 17:34: routes to internet exchanges withdrawn to shift 40 Gbps more. A second 400 Gbps spike came a little after 18:00, already absorbed.

blocks.md:
**Defences, layer by layer.**
- **Remove the amplifiers.** [memcached 1.5.6](https://github.com/memcached/memcached/wiki/ReleaseNotes156), released the day before, "primarily disables the UDP protocol by default". Nothing that answers UDP should face the internet without a reason.
- **Stop spoofing at the source.** BCP 38 (RFC 2827) ingress filtering: providers drop packets whose source address could not come from the customer that sent them. Without spoofing there is no reflection.
- **Absorb and scrub.** A **scrubbing** service (Akamai for GitHub) attracts the traffic via BGP, filters it, and forwards the clean part. **Anycast** (one address announced from many sites, [RFC 4786](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4786)) spreads a flood across all of them, and each site "can act as a sink for attack traffic" from its region.
- **Detect.** CISA advises alerting on "abnormally large responses to a particular IP address", large UDP packets to high ports, and UDP traffic with no matching request.

blocks.code: alert udp any 11211 -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"Possible memcached reflection toward us"; dsize:>1000; threshold: type both, track by_dst, count 100, seconds 10; classtype:attempted-dos; sid:1000103; rev:1;)
blocks.caption: Suricata: large UDP payloads from source port 11211 to our hosts, alerting once per destination when 100 arrive within 10 seconds. We never asked these servers anything, which is the signature of reflection.

blocks.question: A protocol's response is 30 times its request. An attacker wants 300 Gbit/s at the victim. How much spoofed request traffic must they send, and to where?
options: 9,000 Gbit/s, to the reflectors
300 Gbit/s, to the victim
10 Gbit/s, to the victim, with the reflectors' addresses as source
10 Gbit/s, to the reflectors, with the victim's address as source
blocks.explain: Attacker bandwidth is victim bandwidth divided by BAF: 300 / 30 = 10 Gbit/s. The requests go to the reflectors, forged to look as if the victim sent them, so the large answers land on the victim.
