blocks.question: At 17:26 GitHub withdrew its BGP announcements from its transit providers and announced its prefixes only through Akamai. Why did that relieve GitHub's own links?
options: It changed GitHub's IP addresses, so the reflectors lost their target
BGP withdrawal blocks UDP traffic everywhere on the internet
Traffic for GitHub's prefixes now followed routes into Akamai's much larger edge, where filters dropped the flood before it reached GitHub
Akamai asked the memcached servers to stop answering
blocks.explain: BGP decides which networks carry traffic toward a prefix. Announcing only via Akamai made every packet for GitHub, attack included, enter through Akamai, whose capacity absorbed 1.35 Tbps and whose access control lists dropped the memcached responses. The addresses and the reflectors did not change.

lessons.title: Flooding DNS and HTTP/2: Dyn 2016 and Rapid Reset 2023

blocks.md:
Two record-setting attacks show where floods hurt most: at a shared dependency, and at the cost asymmetry inside a protocol.

**Case: Dyn, 21 October 2016.** Dyn was a managed DNS provider: its servers answered as the authoritative name servers for many companies' domains. The prerequisite introduced Mirai, the botnet of hacked cameras and routers. The USENIX Security 2017 study of Mirai reconstructs the Dyn day from the botnet's own commands: "23 attack commands that targeted Dyn infrastructure, from 11:07 to 16:55 UTC". The first 21 were short (about 25 seconds) SYN floods on DNS port 53, with a few ACK and GRE floods, followed by sustained 1-hour and 5-hour SYN floods on TCP port 53. Name resolution failed for Dyn's customers, including Amazon, GitHub, Netflix, PayPal, Reddit and Twitter, although their own servers were fine.

blocks.title: Mirai commands against Dyn, 21 October 2016 (hours UTC)

scenes.caption: From 11:07 UTC: 21 short bursts, about 25 seconds each, mostly SYN floods on port 53 (drawn as one block).
Then sustained 1-hour and 5-hour SYN floods on TCP/53. Exact start times are simplified here; the commands end by 16:55.
At 22:17 UTC a final 10-hour attack hit Dyn and PlayStation infrastructure together, past midnight (the chart is cut at 24:00).

blocks.md:
The paper adds two lessons. First, 107,464 addresses attacked Dyn and 71 percent of them were also seen scanning as Mirai, so "while the attack clearly involved Mirai, there may have been other hosts involved". Second, the targets: the attacked Dyn addresses were the name servers for PlayStation's network, which suggests the attacker "was likely targeting gaming infrastructure that incidentally disrupted service to Dyn's broader customer base". Mirai used direct, non-reflected floods; sheer device count was enough.

**Defender's view:** a domain whose names are served by one DNS provider shares that provider's outages. Serving a zone from more than one provider ([RFC 2182](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2182) asks for name servers on diverse networks, so one provider's failure cannot make them all unreachable), and keeping record TTLs long enough that resolvers can ride out a short outage from cache ([RFC 9199](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9199) cites measurements showing caching protects users through DDoS attacks), both reduce that dependency.

**Case: HTTP/2 Rapid Reset, 2023 (CVE-2023-44487).** HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) carries many requests over one TCP connection as **streams**: numbered, interleaved request and response pairs. A server advertises how many may be open at once with `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` (RFC 9113 recommends no fewer than 100). A client can cancel a stream at any time with a **RST_STREAM** frame, which is useful when a user navigates away from a page.

Google's write-up (Juho Snellman and Daniele Iamartino) explains the trick: open streams and cancel each one immediately. A cancelled stream no longer counts against the limit, so "each connection [can] have an indefinite number of requests in flight", limited only by bandwidth rather than round-trip time. Meanwhile the server still allocates stream state, decompresses headers, maps the URL and may already have forwarded the request to a backend. The client pays almost nothing; that is the cost asymmetry.

blocks.title: Normal HTTP/2 versus Rapid Reset on one connection

scenes.caption: Normal: the client opens up to 100 streams and waits. New streams open only as responses come back, so throughput is about 100 requests per round trip.
Rapid Reset: the client sends a request and cancels it in the same breath. The stream closes, freeing a slot at once.
The proxy has already parsed and decompressed the request, and may have sent it to the backend. That work is wasted, and no response is sent back.
Repeat without waiting for any reply. The concurrency limit never fills, so requests per connection are bounded by bandwidth, not round trips.

blocks.md:
**Scale.** Google reported a peak above **398 million requests per second** in August 2023 ([its largest the year before](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps) was 46 million). [Cloudflare measured](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) just above **201 million** per second from a botnet of "merely 20,000 machines", about 10,050 requests per second from each machine.

**Mitigations**, from Google's analysis: blocking individual requests is not enough; "the entire TCP connection needs to be closed when abuse is detected", using a GOAWAY frame (HTTP/2's "stop opening streams" message) that takes effect immediately rather than the slow graceful form. Abuse is judged from connection statistics, for example "more than 100 requests with more than 50% of the given requests canceled". Servers should also close connections that try to exceed the stream limit. Cloudflare added an "IP Jail" that bars offending addresses from HTTP/2 for a while.

blocks.title: Scoring an HTTP/2 connection for Rapid Reset abuse

scenes.caption: Each connection keeps counters. This is the heuristic Google describes, written as code; real servers tune the thresholds.
A browser that cancelled a few requests (user clicked away): 7 of 150 is under 5 percent.
A bot cancelling almost everything: 150 of 150 is far above half after more than 100 requests. Close the whole connection, not just the stream.
The non-cancelling variant opens more streams than allowed. Repeat offenders get the connection closed too, as Google recommends.

blocks.md: Application-layer floods win through asymmetry: a cheap action for the client (open and cancel a stream) that is expensive for the server. Defences measure behaviour per connection and close abusive connections outright, because per-request blocking leaves the cheap channel open. The pattern recurs: MadeYouReset (CVE-2025-8671, 2025) uses malformed control frames to make the server reset streams itself.

blocks.question: Why does setting SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS lower not stop Rapid Reset?
options: Because RST_STREAM frames are encrypted
Because the limit only applies to HTTP/1.1
Because clients ignore the setting
Because cancelled streams stop counting toward the limit, so the client can keep opening new ones without waiting; the request rate depends on bandwidth, not on the limit
blocks.explain: The limit caps streams that are open at one moment. A stream reset immediately is closed, so the attacker never reaches the cap. Cloudflare's write-up says stream concurrency on its own cannot mitigate rapid reset.

blocks.question: Many unrelated websites failed on 21 October 2016 although their own servers were healthy. What did they have in common?
options: Their domains' authoritative DNS was served by Dyn, so resolvers could not look up their addresses
They all used HTTP/2
They were all infected with Mirai
They all used the same web host
blocks.explain: Mirai flooded Dyn's DNS servers. Users' resolvers could not get answers for those domains once cached records expired, so the sites were unreachable by name even though they were up.

blocks.md:
Before most attacks comes **reconnaissance**: finding which addresses are alive and which ports are open. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as technique T1595.001, scanning IP blocks, ranging "from simple pings (ICMP requests and responses) to more nuanced scans that may reveal host software/versions". Internet-facing addresses are scanned constantly, so the defender's job is not to panic at every scan but to tell background noise from attention aimed at you, and to know your own exposure first.

Tiny example: one outside address touches 1,000 ports on one of your servers in 40 seconds. Three ports answer. What do your logs show?

**What the scanner sends, and what you record.** The prerequisite showed Nmap's default **SYN scan**: send SYN; an open port answers SYN-ACK, a closed port answers RST, and a filtered port (a firewall dropping silently) answers nothing. Nmap's documentation calls it "relatively unobtrusive and stealthy since it never completes TCP connections". It is not invisible to a network sensor.

**Zeek** is a network monitor that turns traffic into structured logs. Its `conn.log` has a `conn_state` and a `history` for every connection attempt. From Zeek's reference: **S0** means "Connection attempt seen, no reply"; **REJ** means "Connection attempt rejected". History letters are upper case for the originator and lower case for the responder: `S` SYN, `h` SYN-ACK, `r`/`R` RST, `a` ACK, `d` data.

- Filtered port: history `S`, state `S0`.
- Closed port: history `Sr`, state `REJ`.
- Open port probed by a SYN scan: history `ShR`, a handshake answered then abandoned by the scanner.

blocks.title: Finding the scanner in conn.log records
blocks.code:
from collections import defaultdict

# (source, destination, dest port, history) from Zeek conn.log, simplified
conns = [
    ("203.0.113.9", "10.0.0.5", 21,   "Sr"),
    ("203.0.113.9", "10.0.0.5", 22,   "ShR"),
    ("203.0.113.9", "10.0.0.5", 23,   "S"),
    ("203.0.113.9", "10.0.0.5", 25,   "Sr"),
    ("203.0.113.9", "10.0.0.5", 443,  "ShR"),
    ("198.51.100.4", "10.0.0.5", 443, "ShADadFf"),
    ("198.51.100.4", "10.0.0.5", 443, "ShADadFf"),
]

ports = defaultdict(set)
unfinished = defaultdict(int)
for src, dst, port, hist in conns:
    ports[src].add(port)
    if "A" not in hist:          # originator never sent a plain ACK
        unfinished[src] += 1

for src in ports:
    print(src, len(ports[src]), "ports,", unfinished[src], "never completed")

scenes.caption: Seven records. Two sources: one touching many ports, one making ordinary HTTPS connections. Addresses are from documentation ranges.
For each source, collect distinct destination ports, and count attempts where the originator never sent an ACK (no 'A' in history).
The first source: 5 distinct ports, all 5 never completed. Closed ports (Sr), a filtered one (S), and open ones it abandoned (ShR).
The second: one port, full handshakes with data and clean FIN closes (ShADadFf). Normal client. Fan-out plus unfinished handshakes is the scan signature.
scenes.output:
203.0.113.9 5 ports, 5 never completed
198.51.100.4 1 ports, 0 never completed

blocks.title: Distinct destination ports per source in one hour (illustrative)

scenes.caption: Illustrative counts. Most sources touch one or two ports. Your own monitoring and authorised scanners touch many, and should be on an allow list.
An unknown outside host touching 1,000 ports looks just like your scanner. The difference is who it is, which is why defenders keep an inventory of authorised scanning.

blocks.md:
**Other views of the same scan.** Firewall logs show a burst of denied packets from one source across many ports. Flow records (lesson 17) show many tiny flows of one or two packets each. An IDS (intrusion detection system, lesson 17) can count, as in the rule below. **Horizontal scans** (one port across many hosts, typical of worms like Mirai hunting for Telnet) look different from **vertical scans** (many ports on one host): count distinct destination hosts per source as well as distinct ports.

**Response.** For outside scans of your internet edge: mostly record and correlate. Act when a scan is followed by connections to the ports it found, when it targets a service you did not know was exposed, or when the source is *inside* your network, because an internal host scanning its neighbours often means it is compromised.

blocks.code: alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"Possible port scan: many SYNs from one source"; flow:stateless; flags:S,12; threshold: type both, track by_src, count 200, seconds 60; classtype:attempted-recon; sid:1000104; rev:1;)
blocks.caption: Suricata: at most one alert per source per minute once it sends 200 SYNs (without ACK) into our network. Exclude your own scanners with a pass rule or by address.

blocks.md: Scan yourself first, with permission and on your own address space, and compare the result to what you believe is exposed. The prerequisite's legal line applies: scanning networks you do not own or have written permission to test can be a crime.

blocks.question: In conn.log you see thousands of records from one internal workstation, each to a different internal IP on port 445, nearly all with history S and state S0. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: Normal file sharing
The workstation's antivirus updating
A horizontal scan from a possibly compromised internal host; most targets did not answer
A SYN flood against the workstation
blocks.explain: One source, one port, many destinations, almost no answers: a horizontal scan, the pattern of worms and of attackers moving laterally. That it comes from inside makes it urgent; isolate and examine the workstation.

blocks.question: A closed port and a filtered port are probed with a SYN. How do they differ in Zeek's conn.log?
options: Closed: history S, state S0. Filtered: history Sr, state REJ.
Closed: history Sr, state REJ. Filtered: history S, state S0.
Both show ShR
Zeek does not log either
blocks.explain: A closed port answers with RST (lower-case r, from the responder), which Zeek records as REJ. A filtered port gives no answer at all, which is S0, a connection attempt with no reply.

blocks.md:
The prerequisite introduced firewalls as rule lists that allow or block traffic. NIST's firewall guide (SP 800-41 Rev. 1; NIST is the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) separates them by how much they remember and understand. That difference decides which of this course's attacks they can stop.

Tiny example: a rule set allows inbound web traffic to a server and replies to connections the server itself started. An attacker sends a packet with only the ACK flag set, pretending to be a reply. Does it get through?

- **Packet filtering (stateless).** Each packet is judged alone on its header: addresses, ports, protocol, flags. NIST: it does not "associate multiple requests within a single session to each other". A typical router access list is a packet filter. To allow replies, such rule sets matched any TCP packet with ACK or RST set (Cisco's `established` keyword), so the forged ACK above passes.
- **Stateful inspection.** The firewall "keeps track of each connection in a state table", recording addresses, ports and connection state, and checks each packet against it. NIST's own example: a packet claiming to be part of an established connection is accepted only if that connection is in the table. The forged ACK is dropped.
- **Application firewalls** add "stateful protocol analysis", which some vendors call deep packet inspection: understanding the application protocol to block, say, executable attachments or a protocol tunnelled over port 80. Vendors sell firewalls that combine stateful inspection, application awareness and intrusion prevention as **next-generation firewalls** (NGFWs).

blocks.title: The same four packets through a stateless and a stateful firewall

scenes.caption: Rules: allow new inbound TCP to port 443; allow replies. Four packets: a real client's SYN to 443, the server's SYN-ACK, a forged lone ACK to port 3389 (ACK*), and the real client's ACK.
Stateless: 'allow replies' can only be written as 'allow TCP with ACK set', so the forged ACK to 3389 passes the filter.
Stateful: the SYN creates a table entry; the SYN-ACK and the client's ACK match it. The forged ACK matches no entry and is dropped as invalid.

blocks.caption: Adapted from the nftables wiki's 'Simple ruleset for a server' page. nftables is the Linux kernel's firewall framework; 'ct state' reads the connection tracking table, which is what makes it stateful.

blocks.md:
**Rules of thumb from NIST SP 800-41:**
- **Deny by default:** "block all inbound and outbound traffic that has not been expressly permitted". The ruleset above does this with `policy drop`.
- **Egress filtering** ("filtering of outgoing network traffic") matters as much as inbound: it stops internal machines from reaching attacker servers, and NIST says outbound traffic with invalid source addresses should be blocked, which is BCP 38 applied at your own edge (no spoofed packets leave your network to join someone else's amplification attack).
- Firewalls keep state, so they can themselves be flooded: a SYN flood or many half-open connections can fill a state table. Protocol floods (lesson 12) target firewalls and load balancers as often as servers.

A firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Firewalls decide who may talk to whom on which port; whether the conversation itself is malicious is the job of the application, TLS, and IDS or application-layer inspection.

blocks.question: A router access list allows 'TCP from any with the ACK flag set' so that replies work. What can an outside attacker do that a stateful firewall would block?
options: Decrypt TLS traffic
Nothing different: both read the ACK flag
Flood the router with SYNs
Send packets with ACK set to any internal port, which pass because the filter cannot check that a real connection exists; useful for probing and some attacks
blocks.explain: A stateless filter has no memory of which connections exist, so any packet with ACK set looks like a reply. A stateful firewall checks its table and drops ACKs that belong to no known connection.

blocks.question: Which rule best implements NIST's egress advice for a company network 192.0.2.0/24?
options: Allow outbound only on port 53
Drop outbound packets whose source address is not in 192.0.2.0/24, and allow only the outbound services the business needs
Drop all inbound traffic
Allow all outbound traffic, since it comes from inside
blocks.explain: Egress filtering drops packets that could not legitimately come from your network (spoofed sources, which feed reflection attacks) and limits outbound services, which hinders malware that needs to reach its controller. Port 53 only would break the business and still allow DNS tunnelling.

lessons.title: Segmentation, zero trust and the Target breach

blocks.md:
**Segmentation** divides a network into zones (with VLANs, subnets and firewalls between them) so that a compromise in one zone does not give access to everything. **Microsegmentation** takes it further: NIST SP 800-207 describes placing "individual or groups of resources on a unique network segment protected by a gateway security component", or enforcing it with software on each host, so that even machines in the same data centre must pass a policy check to talk.

The case that made this a board-level topic is Target, 2013.

**Case: Target, November and December 2013.** The US Senate Commerce Committee's "kill chain" analysis (2014) summarises public reporting: attackers first stole credentials from Fazio Mechanical Services, a refrigeration and HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) contractor that "had remote access to Target's network for electronic billing, contract submission, and project management", by malware-laden email. With them they entered Target's network around 12 November, then moved "from less sensitive areas of Target's network to areas storing consumer data". They installed RAM-scraping malware (it reads card data from a register's memory while briefly unencrypted) on point-of-sale (POS) terminals from 15 November; most were infected by 30 November.

From 2 December stolen data moved through another compromised Target server to outside FTP (File Transfer Protocol) servers: about 11 GB over two weeks. Around 40 million card numbers and up to 70 million customer records were taken. Target learned of it from the US Department of Justice on 12 December.

blocks.title: Target 2013: a flat path from vendor portal to cash registers

scenes.caption: September or earlier: phishing gives the attackers Fazio's credentials for Target's vendor systems (Senate report: at least two months before the breach).
Mid-November: from the vendor-facing edge into the internal network. The Senate report: the outside portal was likely 'not fully isolated from the rest of Target's network'.
15 to 30 November: malware installed on POS terminals. A later Verizon assessment found 'no controls limiting their access to any system', registers included.
From 2 December: card data collected on an internal server and sent out by FTP. The intrusion-detection tool alerted; nobody acted. Egress filtering should have blocked FTP to the internet.
With segmentation: vendor access confined to the billing systems, POS in its own zone that accepts only what registers need, and no direct outbound FTP. Each red edge would need a separate breach.

blocks.md:
**What the investigations found.** Brian Krebs, an investigative security journalist, [later reported](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2015/09/inside-target-corp-days-after-2013-breach/) excerpts of Verizon's confidential post-breach assessment for Target: its consultants "were able to directly communicate with point-of-sale registers and servers from the core network", in one case reaching checkout-lane registers after compromising "a deli meat scale located in a different store". They also cracked 472,308 of 547,470 Target passwords (86 percent) within a week.

The Senate report adds the detection failure: Target's FireEye intrusion detection system "triggered urgent alerts with each installation of the data exfiltration malware", and Target's security team "neither reacted to the alarms nor allowed the FireEye software to automatically delete the malware". Lesson: segmentation slows attackers down; detection only helps if someone acts.

**Zero trust.** Segmentation still trusts whatever is inside a zone. **Zero trust** (NIST SP 800-207) "assumes there is no implicit trust granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location". Three of its seven tenets carry the networking idea:

- "All communication is secured regardless of network location." Inside traffic is encrypted and authenticated like outside traffic.
- "Access to individual enterprise resources is granted on a per-session basis", with least privilege; access to one resource does not grant another.
- Access is decided by "dynamic policy", including the device's state, not just the user's password.

Architecturally, a **policy decision point** (PDP) decides and a **policy enforcement point** (PEP), such as a gateway, proxy or host agent, enforces, in front of every resource.

blocks.title: Zero trust: every session is checked, inside or not

scenes.caption: A vendor technician's laptop asks for the billing application. Being on the network grants nothing by itself.
The gateway asks the policy engine: who is this, is the device healthy, is this resource allowed for this role, now?
Allowed for this session only, to this application only.
The same laptop then tries to reach a POS management server. A new request, a new decision: denied. This is the check Target's vendor path lacked.

blocks.md: Segmentation limits how far one compromise spreads; zero trust removes network location as a reason to trust anything. Both assume a breach will happen, and both only pay off when someone watches the alerts at the boundaries.

blocks.question: Target's attackers entered with a vendor's credentials. Which control would most directly have stopped them reaching cash registers, even with those credentials?
options: Longer passwords for Target's staff
Segmenting vendor access so it could reach only the billing and project systems, with the POS zone accepting no connections from there
A faster internet connection
Antivirus on the vendor's computers
blocks.explain: The credentials were valid; the failure was what they could reach. Confining vendor access and isolating the POS zone means a stolen vendor login stays a billing-system problem. The other measures help elsewhere but do not cut the path.

blocks.question: Which statement matches NIST SP 800-207's idea of zero trust?
options: Every access request is authenticated and authorised per session, using policy that includes device state, regardless of where on the network it comes from
Devices inside the corporate network are trusted; outside ones are not
Once a user logs in to the VPN, they may access any internal system
Zero trust means blocking all traffic
blocks.explain: Zero trust removes implicit trust from network location. The log-in-to-the-VPN model is exactly the implicit trust zone it replaces. It does not mean blocking everything, but deciding each session explicitly.

lessons.title: Intrusion detection, network monitoring, and where to practise

blocks.md:
Every lesson so far ended with "what defenders see". This lesson is about the systems that see it. An **IDS** (intrusion detection system) watches traffic and raises alerts; an **IPS** (intrusion prevention system) sits in the traffic path and can also block. [NIST SP 800-94](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-94.pdf) describes the two placements: an **inline** sensor is one the traffic "must pass through", deployed so that it can stop attacks; a **passive** sensor "monitors a copy of the actual network traffic", for example from a switch's spanning (mirror) port or a network tap.

Tiny example: the memcached rule from lesson 12 running on a passive sensor raises an alert; the same rule set to `drop` on an inline sensor discards the packets.

NIST SP 800-94 names the main detection methods:

- **Signature-based:** compare activity with patterns of known threats. "Very effective at detecting known threats but largely ineffective at detecting previously unknown threats", and easily missed by small variations.
- **Anomaly-based:** compare activity with a profile of normal behaviour built over a training period ("typically days, sometimes weeks"). It can catch new attacks, but it produces many false positives when normal behaviour changes, and a patient attacker can slowly train the profile to accept their activity.
- **Stateful protocol analysis:** check traffic against how the protocol is supposed to behave.

Every detector trades **false positives** (benign activity flagged) against **false negatives** (attacks missed): in NIST's words, "reducing the occurrences of one increases the occurrences of the other".

**The tools.** **Snort** is the long-standing open-source signature IDS; CISA's amplification alert quotes a Snort rule. **Suricata** is a newer open-source IDS and IPS engine whose rules follow the same shape (its [documentation](https://docs.suricata.io/en/latest/rules/intro.html) has a section on differences from Snort). **Zeek** is a network monitor that does not primarily alert; it turns traffic into structured logs (`conn.log`, `dns.log`, `http.log` and others) that analysts search and that other tools build detections on. Many teams run Suricata and Zeek side by side on the same passive sensor.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a Suricata rule (split across lines to read)

scenes.caption: Action: alert (others include drop on an inline IPS, and pass). Suricata's docs: a rule is an action, a header and options.
Header: protocol dns (Suricata checks it really is DNS, whatever the port), source network and port, direction, destination network and port.
msg is the alert text an analyst reads. dns.query is a sticky buffer: the following match applies to the query name.
bsize:>60 matches query names longer than 60 bytes. threshold limits noise: alert once per source after 20 matches in 300 seconds.
classtype groups alerts; sid is the rule's unique ID (local rules use high numbers) and rev its version.

blocks.md:
**Flow monitoring.** Full packet capture everywhere is expensive. **NetFlow** (Cisco's format, version 9 documented in RFC 3954) and its IETF successor **IPFIX** (IP Flow Information Export, RFC 7011) instead summarise traffic as **flows**: a flow is "a set of IP packets passing an Observation Point in the network during a certain time interval" that share common properties, typically the 5-tuple. Routers and switches export flow records with addresses, ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, timestamps and interfaces to a **collector**.

Flows cannot show content, but they answer the questions that most of this course's attacks raise: who talked to whom, how much, how often. Scans appear as fan-out of tiny flows; reflection as huge inbound UDP flows from port 11211 or 123 that you never asked for; exfiltration as an unusual outbound volume (Target's 11 GB of FTP); beaconing as small flows at regular intervals.

blocks.code:
# Illustrative flow records (NetFlow/IPFIX fields), as a collector might print them
start               proto src:port             dst:port            pkts   bytes
2026-11-02 10:00:01 UDP   198.51.100.20:11211  192.0.2.80:443      9120   12.1M   # reflection, unasked
2026-11-02 10:00:01 TCP   203.0.113.9:51514    192.0.2.15:22          1      44   # one of 1,000 scan flows
2026-11-02 10:00:05 TCP   10.0.7.31:49822      203.0.113.200:21     310    1.1M   # internal host to outside FTP
2026-11-02 10:01:05 UDP   10.0.4.17:53022      10.0.0.53:53             1      98   # long query every 60 s
blocks.caption: Invented values for teaching; each line matches a pattern from this course. Real collectors add interfaces, TCP flags and AS numbers.

blocks.md: Detection is a pipeline: sensors (Suricata, Zeek, flow exporters) produce signals, analysts and rules turn signals into decisions, and the decision must reach someone who acts. Target had the alert; the pipeline broke at the last step.

**Wi-Fi.** Wireless networks bring their own versions of this course's attacks (rogue access points, deauthentication floods, attacks on the handshake that sets up encryption). They are covered in the **Wireless and mobile security** course; everything here about positions, encryption and monitoring still applies.

**Practise legally**, only on systems you own or platforms built for it:
- Analyse real captures from the [Wireshark sample captures](https://wiki.wireshark.org/SampleCaptures) page: find ARP, DNS and TCP handshakes, then look for this course's patterns.
- Work through traffic-analysis exercises at [malware-traffic-analysis.net](https://www.malware-traffic-analysis.net/), which publishes pcaps of real infections with answers.
- Try the network forensics and IDS challenges on [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/).
- Read Zeek's [conn.log](https://docs.zeek.org/en/master/logs/conn.html) and [dns.log](https://docs.zeek.org/en/master/logs/dns.html) guides and run Zeek on your own captures.

blocks.question: An anomaly-based detector was trained during a week when an attacker was already quietly exfiltrating data. What is the risk?
options: The detector will block all traffic
Signatures will be deleted
The attacker's traffic becomes part of the 'normal' profile, so it will not be flagged
None, anomaly detection catches everything new
blocks.explain: NIST SP 800-94 warns that malicious activity observed while profiles are built gets included as normal. That is a classic false negative source, and one reason to combine anomaly detection with signatures and with review of what 'normal' contains.

blocks.question: You need to detect large outbound transfers from any internal host to the internet across a big network, cheaply. Which data source fits best?
options: Full packet capture on every switch port
Antivirus logs
Flow records (NetFlow or IPFIX) exported from border routers to a collector
DNSSEC signatures
blocks.explain: Flows summarise who sent how many bytes to whom without storing content, so they are cheap enough to keep for the whole network and long periods, and outbound volume per host is exactly what they measure.

blocks.question: A Suricata sensor is connected to a switch's mirror port. A rule with action 'drop' matches an attack. What happens?
options: Nothing is blocked: a passive sensor sees copies of traffic, so it can alert but not stop the original packets
The rule fails to load
The attack packets are dropped
The switch shuts the port
blocks.explain: A sensor on a mirror (spanning) port is passive by definition: it receives copies. Blocking requires an inline deployment where traffic must pass through the sensor, as NIST SP 800-94 describes.
